title: Ansel and the Will
premise: Hazel Iversen, an insurance investigator whose photographic memory has made her the unofficial archivist of her small town's secrets, is hired by a nervous stranger who pays triple to prove that a murder will not happen — a murder scheduled, by implication of an old will, for the coming month. The case traces back to the death of Edith Marlowe twelve years ago, ruled accidental, whose contested will is about to be re-opened in probate court. As Hazel reconstructs the original night using only what she remembers seeing and filing away, she realizes the town's most respected citizens buried the truth together — and that her own late father helped them. The killer, now a candidate beneficiary under the revived will, plans to make the 'predicted' murder real to close the loophole forever; Hazel must expose the twelve-year-old crime before the trial begins, choosing justice outside the law over the belonging she has always quietly craved.
about_author: Jude Crane spent a decade as a claims adjuster in rural New England before turning to fiction, drawing on the strange paperwork of ordinary grief. They write from a converted records office in Vermont, where they still alphabetize everything.

chapters.title: Paid in Advance
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. A pale, anonymous client walks into Iversen Claims & Research and pays three months upfront to prove a murder hasn't happened yet — naming no victim, only a date six weeks out. Hazel's memory flags his cologne as one she's filed before. Emotional beat: unease dressed up as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Small Towns
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Establishing her method: twelve years of index cards, photographs, and overheard confessions filed by name. She searches her mental archive for the client's face and finds it adjacent to a funeral notice from 2013. Beat: the comfort of order beginning to crack.

chapters.title: Edith Marlowe, Deceased, Accidentally
chapters.summary: Hazel pulls the old file: Edith Marlowe fell down her cellar stairs twelve years ago; the insurance paid without dispute. But the file contains a page Hazel remembers photographing that was never returned. POV shifts briefly to Deputy Coroner Ruth Okafor's recollection. Beat: first hard evidence of tampering.

chapters.title: The Will That Wouldn't Die
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Probate court re-opens the Marlowe estate because a second will surfaced — dated after Edith's death, impossible unless someone forged it or someone knew she'd die. The beneficiaries list reads like Hazel's own index cards. Beat: dread; the town's faces and its crimes are the same faces.

chapters.title: Client Unknown
chapters.summary: Hazel tails her client to the Marlowe house and loses him, but memorizes every car on the street. One belongs to Councilman Aldous Vane, executor of the original estate. Beat: paranoia; Hazel realizes being invisible made her the perfect witness all along.

chapters.title: What My Father Filed
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, at her father's grave and then his old storage unit. She finds his copy of the missing page — a witness statement he notarized the night Edith died, then sealed. Her father helped bury something. Beat: betrayal across the grave; grief weaponized into resolve.

chapters.title: Ruth Remembers Falling
chapters.summary: Ruth Okafor's POV. The retired deputy coroner admits the body had ligature bruising the family begged her to omit; her granddaughter's college fund came from an anonymous gift soon after. Beat: complicity confessed, guilt calcified into silence.

chapters.title: Six Weeks Out
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. She maps the client's predicted date against the trial calendar: the new will's validity hearing falls exactly on it. Someone intends a death that will invalidate the will permanently. Beat: the mystery becomes a countdown.

chapters.title: The Beneficiaries Club
chapters.summary: Hazel attends the wake-style gathering of would-be heirs and memorizes every lie told about where they were twelve years ago. Two alibis contradict her archived photographs. Beat: cold satisfaction of catching people in their own pasts.

chapters.title: A Threat, Politely Worded
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. An anonymous letter offers to buy her entire archive; the offer doubles when she declines, then turns explicit about her father's role. Beat: fear, and the sting of her father's ghost being used against her.

chapters.title: Fire at the Records Office
chapters.summary: Third-person limited through Hazel's neighbor Danny. A fire guts the county annex where the original coroner's report is stored; Danny sees a man with a distinctive cologne leaving. Beat: escalation — the past is being destroyed faster than Hazel can recover it.

chapters.title: The Photograph in My Head
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Interrogating her own flawless memory of the night Edith died — she was seventeen, delivering papers, and saw a second car. She reconstructs the license plate digit by digit. Beat: her gift transforms from burden to instrument.

chapters.title: Vane's Version
chapters.summary: Councilman Vane's POV. He explains — sincerely believing it — how covering up Edith's 'accident' protected the town's largest employer. Beat: chilling banality; the antagonist's logic almost makes sense.

chapters.title: The Client Comes Clean
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Her client reveals himself: Edith's estranged grandson, who received anonymous letters predicting his own murder on the hearing date — letters written in Edith's hand, though she's been dead twelve years. Beat: the mystery pivots from whodunit to who's-still-doing-it.

chapters.title: Letters from the Dead
chapters.summary: Hazel analyzes the letters and matches the handwriting to someone who learned it from Edith: her live-in nurse, Miriam Ashe, listed nowhere in either will. Beat: revelation with a hollow center — motive still missing.

chapters.title: Miriam's Room
chapters.summary: Hazel and the grandson break into Miriam's abandoned cottage and find twelve years of surveillance files on every beneficiary — including Hazel's father, whose statement Miriam witnessed before he sealed it. Beat: vertigo; the watcher was watched.

chapters.title: Midnight at the Marlowe House
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Following Miriam's pattern, Hazel stakes out the Marlowe house and witnesses Vane and the town lawyer burying a strongbox — the original unaltered will, which names Miriam as sole heir if Edith's death proved unnatural. Beat: everything inverts; the cover-up created the killer.

chapters.title: What My Father Knew
chapters.summary: Hazel opens her father's sealed envelope at last: his statement proves Edith was murdered, meaning Miriam inherits — and means everyone who buried the truth, including him, funded their own ruin. Beat: sorrow braided with clarity; forgiveness declined.

chapters.title: The Date Arrives
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge on the eve of the hearing. Miriam, exposed and cornered, takes the grandson hostage in the Marlowe cellar — the same stairs. Hazel walks in carrying only her memory and the evidence. Beat: terror, deliberate and chosen.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Proof
chapters.summary: Climax. Hazel recites, verbatim, every archived fact binding each conspirator to the cover-up, breaking their united front while recording everything; Ruth turns state's witness, and Vane confesses to save himself. Miriam is arrested; the grandson lives. Beat: justice achieved entirely outside a courtroom.

chapters.title: Exhibit A
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The trial begins with her archive entered as evidence; the town must hear its own secrets read aloud in alphabetical order. Some neighbors thank her; some never speak to her again. Beat: cost tallied honestly.

chapters.title: Filed Under Belonging
chapters.summary: Hazel's final chapter. She donates the archive to the public library, keeps only one card — her father's — and accepts the grandson's invitation to Sunday dinner. Invisible no longer, she discovers being known is survivable. Beat: quiet, earned peace.
